Lahore[d] is the capital and largest city of the Pakistani province of Punjab. It is the second-largest city in Pakistan, after Karachi, and 27th largest in the world, with a population of over 14 million.[17] Lahore is one of the country's major industrial, educational and economic hubs,[12][13] and is considered the historic capital and cultural centre of the wider Punjab region.[18][19][20]
The site of the city has been inhabited for over two millennia, although Lahore itself rose to prominence in the late 10th century.[21] At times Lahore has served as the capital of several empires, including the Odi Shahi dynasty, Ghaznavid Empire and Delhi Sultanate. It was one of the principal cities in the Mughal Empire, being its capital city during the reign of Akbar. During this period, it was one of the largest cities in the world.[22] In the 18th century Lahore fell into a period of decay while being contested among the Durranis and the Sikhs; it regained some of its former grandeur when it became capital of the Sikh Kingdom of Lahore in the early 19th century. It was annexed by the East India Company in 1849 and became the capital of Punjab Province.[23] Lahore was central to the independence movements of British India, with the city being the site of both the Declaration of Indian Independence and the resolution for the establishment of Pakistan. It suffered rioting during the partition of British India in 1947.[24] Following the independence of Pakistan, Lahore remained the capital of Punjab province.

Lahore is located in central-eastern Punjab, along the Ravi River, and has a strong cultural and political influence over the country being capital of its most populated province.[25] It is considered a major socially liberal,[26] progressive,[27] and cosmopolitan city in the country.[28] It is a UNESCO City of Literature and major centre for Pakistan's publishing industry, and is as such a foremost centre of Pakistan's literary scene. The city is also a major centre of education,[29] with some of the country's leading universities based there.[30] Lahore is home to Pakistan's Punjabi film industry, and is a major centre of Qawwali music.[31] The city hosts a significant portion of Pakistan's tourism industry,[31][32] with major attractions including the Walled City, the Badshahi and Wazir Khan mosques, as well as several Sikh and Sufi shrines. Lahore is also home to the Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens, both of which are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.[32]
Etymology  
Main article: Etymology of Lahore
The origin of Lahore's name is unclear. The city's name has been variously recorded by early Muslim historians as Luhawar, Lūhār, and Rahwar.[33] The Iranian polymath and geographer, Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, referred to the city as Luhāwar in his 11th century work, Qanun,[33] while the poet Amir Khusrow, who lived during the Delhi Sultanate period, recorded the city's name as Lāhanūr.[34] Yaqut al-Hamawi records the city's name as Lawhūr, mentioning that it was famously known as Lahāwar.[35] Persian historian Firishta mentions the city as Alahwar in his work, with al-Ahwar being another variation.[36][37]
One theory suggests that Lahore's name is a corruption of the word Ravāwar, as R to L shifts are common in languages derived from Sanskrit.[38] Ravāwar is the simplified pronunciation of the name Iravatyāwar, a name possibly derived from the Ravi River, known as the Iravati River in the Vedas.[38][39] Another theory suggests the city's name may derive from the word Lohar, meaning "blacksmith".[40]

The city's location near the Indian border meant that it received large numbers of refugees fleeing eastern Punjab and northern India, though it was able to accommodate them given the large stock of abandoned Hindu and Sikh properties that could be re-distributed to newly arrived refugees.[116] In post-partition India, the loss of Lahore catalyzed the development of the new modernist capital city of Chandigarh.[117]

After independence, Lahore slowly regained its significance as an economic and cultural centre of western Punjab. Lahore[d] is the capital and largest city of the Pakistani province of Punjab. It is the second-largest city in Pakistan, after Karachi, and 27th largest in the world, with a population of over 14 million.[17] Lahore is one of the country's major industrial, educational and economic hubs,[12][13] and is considered the historic capital and cultural centre of the wider Punjab region.[18][19][20]
The site of the city has been inhabited for over two millennia, although Lahore itself rose to prominence in the late 10th century.[21] At times Lahore has served as the capital of several empires, including the Odi Shahi dynasty, Ghaznavid Empire and Delhi Sultanate. It was one of the principal cities in the Mughal Empire, being its capital city during the reign of Akbar. During this period, it was one of the largest cities in the world.[22] In the 18th century Lahore fell into a period of decay while being contested among the Durranis and the Sikhs; it regained some of its former grandeur when it became capital of the Sikh Kingdom of Lahore in the early 19th century. It was annexed by the East India Company in 1849 and became the capital of Punjab Province.[23] Lahore was central to the independence movements of British India, with the city being the site of both the Declaration of Indian Independence and the resolution for the establishment of Pakistan. It suffered rioting during the partition of British India in 1947.[24] Following the independence of Pakistan, Lahore remained the capital of Punjab province.
texts.3:
Lahore is located in central-eastern Punjab, along the Ravi River, and has a strong cultural and political influence over the country being capital of its most populated province.[25] It is considered a major socially liberal,[26] progressive,[27] and cosmopolitan city in the country.[28] It is a UNESCO City of Literature and major centre for Pakistan's publishing industry, and is as such a foremost centre of Pakistan's literary scene. The city is also a major centre of education,[29] with some of the country's leading universities based there.[30] Lahore is home to Pakistan's Punjabi film industry, and is a major centre of Qawwali music.[31] The city hosts a significant portion of Pakistan's tourism industry,[31][32] with major attractions including the Walled City, the Badshahi and Wazir Khan mosques, as well as several Sikh and Sufi shrines. Lahore is also home to the Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens, both of which are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.[32]
Etymology  
Main article: Etymology of Lahore
The origin of Lahore's name is unclear. The city's name has been variously recorded by early Muslim historians as Luhawar, Lūhār, and Rahwar.[33] The Iranian polymath and geographer, Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, referred to the city as Luhāwar in his 11th century work, Qanun,[33] while the poet Amir Khusrow, who lived during the Delhi Sultanate period, recorded the city's name as Lāhanūr.[34] Yaqut al-Hamawi records the city's name as Lawhūr, mentioning that it was famously known as Lahāwar.[35] Persian historian Firishta mentions the city as Alahwar in his work, with al-Ahwar being another variation.[36][37]
One theory suggests that Lahore's name is a corruption of the word Ravāwar, as R to L shifts are common in languages derived from Sanskrit.[38] Ravāwar is the simplified pronunciation of the name Iravatyāwar, a name possibly derived from the Ravi River, known as the Iravati River in the Vedas.[38][39] Another theory suggests the city's name may derive from the word Lohar, meaning "blacksmith".[40]

**Ludhiana** (Panjabi: _Ludhiāṇā_, pronounced[[lʊ́d̪͜tɪ̀ɪˈäːɳäː]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Punjabi "Help:IPA/Punjabi")) is the most populous city in the Indian state of Punjab.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-164.100.161.224-11) The city has an estimated population of 1,618,879 as of the2011 census and distributed over 310 km 2 (120 sq mi),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-District-6) making Ludhiana the most densely populated urban centre in the state.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-12) It is a major industrial centre of Northern India, referred to as "India's Manchester" by the BBC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-13) It is also known as the commercial capital of Punjab.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-164.100.161.224-11)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-15)
It stands on the old bank of Sutlej River, that is now 13 kilometres (8.1 mi) to the south of its present course. The Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs has placed Ludhiana on the 48th position among the top 100 smart cities,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-16) and the city has been ranked as one of the easiest cities in India for business according to the World Bank.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-17)

Although the area around present-day Ludhiana had been inhabited since ancient times, the modern city was established during the late fifteenth century under the Lodi dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. Prior to its foundation, the region comprised several agricultural settlements located along the southern bank of the Sutlej River, whose course has since shifted further north.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-ludhiana.nic.in-18)
During the rule of the Tughlaq dynasty, a fort was constructed to protect the strategic route linking Delhi with north-western India. The fort was captured by the Khokhar ruler Jasrat during his campaign in Punjab in 1421–22, illustrating the declining authority of the Delhi Sultanate in the region.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-19)
Ludhiana was founded in 1480 during the reign of the Lodi dynasty.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-Britannica-20) According to tradition, Sultan Sikandar Lodi sent two military commanders, Yusuf Khan and Nihad Khan, to restore Lodi authority in Punjab. While Yusuf Khan crossed the Sutlej River and established Sultanpur Lodhi, Nihad Khan founded Ludhiana at the village of Mir Hota.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-21).
The city's name was originally _Lodi-ana_, meaning "the town of the Lodis", which gradually evolved into _Lodiana_ and eventually _Ludhiana_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-ludhiana.nic.in-18)
The Lodhi Fort, popularly known as _Purana Qila_, is the only surviving monument from the city's foundation. It was repaired during the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and later maintained by the British administration before falling into disrepair after independence. In December 2013, it was declared a state-protected monument by the Government of Punjab.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-22)

According to the 2011 Census of India, Punjabi is the predominant mother tongue in Ludhiana, spoken by 67.00% of the city's population. Hindi is the second most common first language, accounting for 29.24% of the population, while Bhojpuri is spoken by 1.35%. The remaining 2.41% of residents reported other mother tongues, reflecting the city's linguistic diversity.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-languages-50)
As Punjab's largest industrial and manufacturing centre, Ludhiana has experienced significant in-migration from other parts of India, particularly Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. Consequently, Hindi serves as an important link language in commerce, industry and inter-state communication, while Bhojpuri and several other regional languages are also spoken among migrant communities.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-52)

### Partition and post-independence
Punjabi, written in the Gurmukhi script, is the official language of Punjab and is the principal language of administration, education and local governance in Ludhiana. English is widely used for higher education, judicial proceedings, business and official correspondence, while Hindi is commonly understood and spoken throughout the city owing to its diverse population.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-53)
The municipal administration of Ludhiana began with the establishment of the Municipal Council in 1870. Following the Partition of India in 1947, the city gained strategic importance because of its central location in the reorganised Punjab and emerged as a major industrial centre. Following rapid population growth and urban expansion, the Municipal Corporation of Ludhiana was constituted in 1976 under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1976, replacing the earlier municipal council.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-54) It corporation is responsible for the provision and maintenance of civic infrastructure and public services, including roads, street lighting, water supply, sewerage, sanitation, solid waste management, public health, parks, and urban planning.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-Hindustan_Times_23_July_2021-55)
The administration of the Ludhiana Municipal Corporation is headed by the Municipal Commissioner, Mr. Ojasvi Alankar, IAS.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-56) The Corporation governs an area of 159.37 km² (61.53 sq mi)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-Website-1-57)

**Ludhiana** (Panjabi: _Ludhiāṇā_, pronounced[[lʊ́d̪͜tɪ̀ɪˈäːɳäː]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Punjabi "Help:IPA/Punjabi")) is the most populous city in the Indian state of Punjab.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-164.100.161.224-11) The city has an estimated population of 1,618,879 as of the2011 census and distributed over 310 km 2 (120 sq mi),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-District-6) making Ludhiana the most densely populated urban centre in the state.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-12) It is a major industrial centre of Northern India, referred to as "India's Manchester" by the BBC.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-13) It is also known as the commercial capital of Punjab.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-164.100.161.224-11)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-15)
It stands on the old bank of Sutlej River, that is now 13 kilometres (8.1 mi) to the south of its present course. The Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs has placed Ludhiana on the 48th position among the top 100 smart cities,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-16) and the city has been ranked as one of the easiest cities in India for business according to the World Bank.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-17)
texts.3:
Although the area around present-day Ludhiana had been inhabited since ancient times, the modern city was established during the late fifteenth century under the Lodi dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. Prior to its foundation, the region comprised several agricultural settlements located along the southern bank of the Sutlej River, whose course has since shifted further north.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-ludhiana.nic.in-18)
During the rule of the Tughlaq dynasty, a fort was constructed to protect the strategic route linking Delhi with north-western India. The fort was captured by the Khokhar ruler Jasrat during his campaign in Punjab in 1421–22, illustrating the declining authority of the Delhi Sultanate in the region.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-19)
Ludhiana was founded in 1480 during the reign of the Lodi dynasty.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-Britannica-20) According to tradition, Sultan Sikandar Lodi sent two military commanders, Yusuf Khan and Nihad Khan, to restore Lodi authority in Punjab. While Yusuf Khan crossed the Sutlej River and established Sultanpur Lodhi, Nihad Khan founded Ludhiana at the village of Mir Hota.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-21).
The city's name was originally _Lodi-ana_, meaning "the town of the Lodis", which gradually evolved into _Lodiana_ and eventually _Ludhiana_.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-ludhiana.nic.in-18)
The Lodhi Fort, popularly known as _Purana Qila_, is the only surviving monument from the city's foundation. It was repaired during the reign of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and later maintained by the British administration before falling into disrepair after independence. In December 2013, it was declared a state-protected monument by the Government of Punjab.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-22)

According to the 2011 Census of India, Punjabi is the predominant mother tongue in Ludhiana, spoken by 67.00% of the city's population. Hindi is the second most common first language, accounting for 29.24% of the population, while Bhojpuri is spoken by 1.35%. The remaining 2.41% of residents reported other mother tongues, reflecting the city's linguistic diversity.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-languages-50)
As Punjab's largest industrial and manufacturing centre, Ludhiana has experienced significant in-migration from other parts of India, particularly Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. Consequently, Hindi serves as an important link language in commerce, industry and inter-state communication, while Bhojpuri and several other regional languages are also spoken among migrant communities.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-52)

### Partition and post-independence
Punjabi, written in the Gurmukhi script, is the official language of Punjab and is the principal language of administration, education and local governance in Ludhiana. English is widely used for higher education, judicial proceedings, business and official correspondence, while Hindi is commonly understood and spoken throughout the city owing to its diverse population.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-53)
The municipal administration of Ludhiana began with the establishment of the Municipal Council in 1870. Following the Partition of India in 1947, the city gained strategic importance because of its central location in the reorganised Punjab and emerged as a major industrial centre. Following rapid population growth and urban expansion, the Municipal Corporation of Ludhiana was constituted in 1976 under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1976, replacing the earlier municipal council.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-54) It corporation is responsible for the provision and maintenance of civic infrastructure and public services, including roads, street lighting, water supply, sewerage, sanitation, solid waste management, public health, parks, and urban planning.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-Hindustan_Times_23_July_2021-55)
The administration of the Ludhiana Municipal Corporation is headed by the Municipal Commissioner, Mr. Ojasvi Alankar, IAS.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-56) The Corporation governs an area of 159.37 km² (61.53 sq mi)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludhiana#cite_note-Website-1-57)
